title: C++ - Bitwise operations
description:
C++ lets you operate directly on binary. A binary number literal is just `0b<binary number>`. Binary is also known as base 2. (rightmost bit is smallest), and doubles in size per bit. A bit is a 1/0 and a byte is 8 bits. So 1 byte is 8 chars, and if bit 1 = 128, bit 2 = 64, bit 3 = 32, bit 4 = 16... so `0b11111111` = 255.

---
## Bitwise operators
In C++, there are 6 bitwise operators.
1. `a << b` (LShift). This binary shifts a number (a) b bits. One shift left is equal to multiplying by 2, so 64 (`0b1000000`) << 1 = 128.
2. `a >> b` (RShift). LShift but right. A 1 bit RShift = divide by 2. 128 (`0b10000000`) >> 1 = 64.
3. `a & b` (Binary AND). You already have and, but that just treats values as true or false. Binary and ands each individual bit. To show: 214 (`0b11010110`) & 78 (`0b01001110`) = 70(`0b01000110`)
4. `a | b` (Binary OR). Binary or ors each individual bit, so 214 (`0b11010110`) | 78 (`0b01001110`) = 222 (`0b11011110`)
5. `a ^ b` (Binary XOR): A XOR (Exclusive OR) is true when one but not both bits are true. 214 (`0b11010110`) ^ 78 (`0b01001110`) = 152 (`0b10011000`)
6. `~a` (Binary NOT): Nots each bit, so ~214 (`0b11010110`) = 41 (`0b00101001`) (all of these examples are unsigned. How negative numbers work is that the most significant bit (so 128 in a byte) actually means the negative version, so it = -128 (in a byte). That means that in a unsigned byte, one bytes max is 255, but in signed, one bytes max is 127 and min is -128)
Of course, you can overload bitwise ops just like any other.
